newsitem.title: MEXICO: Cemex seen fending off U.S. rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Cemex seen fending off U.S. rate hike.

text.p: Mexico's heavily indebted cement manufacturer Cemex could clear the hurdle of an expected rise in U.S. interest rates, analysts said.

"Of Cemex's dollar-denominated debt, 75 percent is at a fixed rate and the other 25 percent is at Libor plus a spread," Paul Rodriguez, an equity analyst with Caspian Securities told Reuters on Thursday.
"But Libor is not directly linked to U.S. long-bond yields, and Libor does not respond swiftly to a change in U.S. rates," added Rodriguez, who reiterated his buy rating for Cemex.

Cemex has a total debt of $5.405 billion, of which almost 97 percent is denominated in dollars. The stock has traded nervously in recent sessions on fears debt payments would increase sharply in the wake of a U.S. interest-rate rise expected at Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting. Bear Stearns analyst Sobani Warner estimated a rise in U.S. base rates would hit Cemex's earnings, but said the impact would be limited.

"Regarding Cemex's sensitivity to U.S. rates, we estimate that roughly $1.5 billion of debt would immediately be affected by a change in rates. A 100 basis-point upward move in rates lowers cash earnings by roughly three cents (per share), roughly four percent," Warner wrote in a Bear Stearns report published March 19.
Cemex's Chief Financial Officer Rodrigo Trevio told Reuters on Thursday the company was negotiating a $600 million credit rollover with a banking syndicate to meet debt maturities due in 1997.
Cemex is negotiating with Chase Manhattan, JP Morgan, Citibank and Bankers Trust, Trevio said.
"As and when we have this credit line available, access to other sources of financing will be more attractive," he said.
Luis Antonio de Len, an analyst with the Valores Finamex brokerage in Mexico City said the credit rollover would greatly help Cemex meet its 1997 debt obligations.
"With this (the rollover), they are almost there and even if they are not, with the $600 million guarantee, what's left is easy," de Len said on Thursday.
